full_judgment:
On an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure this Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1-11 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 15.07.2009 passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Netrokona in Other Class Appeal No.189 of 2006 and affirming the judgment and decree dated 20.09.2006 passed by the Assistant Judge, Madar, Netrokona in Other Class Suit No.25 of 2004 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

Facts in short are that the opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted above suit for recovery of possession of 2.64 acres land as described fully in the schedule to the plaint alleging that above property belonged to Bhupendra Chakrabarty and predecessor of the plaintiff Nos.1-3 purchased 1.69 acres land from above Bhupendra Chakrabarty by three registered kabala deed Nos.2574, 2576 and 2577 dated 16.10.1976. They also purchased land of Plot No.2599 from Joynal who in his turm purchased the same from Bhupendra Chakrabarty. The father of plaintiff No.1 filed Title Suit No.180 of 1989 against the Government and the defendant of this suit and obtained a decree and above defendants preferred Other Class Appeal No.100 of 1991 which was disposed on compromise on 17.08.1994. Predecessor of the plaintiff Nos.1-9 namely Janab Hossain gave oral permission to defendant No.1 to erect a dwelling hut in a part of above disputed land. On 23.05.2004 defendant Nos.1 and 2 prohibited the plaintiffs from catching fish from the pond of the disputed land.

Above suit was contested by defendant Nos.1, 2 and 4 by filing two separate written statement. Defendant No.1 claimed that he obtained settlement of 14 decimal land of Plot No.2599 from the Government vide Settlement Case No. 1505(XII) 99-2000 /202(XII) 99-2000 and they are possessing above land by mutating their names and paying rent to the Government. Above defendant purchased 83 decimal land out of above disputed property by registered kabala deed dated 02.02.1971 from Purno Chandra Chakrabarty and he is possessing above land by constructing his dwelling house, excavating a tank and growing trees. Defendant was not a permissive possess Janab Hossain or of the plaintiffs and plaintiffs did not have any title and possession in above land.

Defendant No.4 Government of Bangladesh represented by Deputy Commissioner, Netrokona stated that 14 decimals land of Plot No.2599 was rightly recorded in the name of the Government in S.A. Khatian No.1 and the Government gave settlement of above land to defendant No.1. Plaintiffs do not have any right, title and possession in above land.

At trial plaintiffs examined 3 witnesses and their documents were marked as Exhibit Nos.1-7. On the other hand defendants examined 4 witnesses and their documents were marked as Exhibit Nos.’Ka’ – ‘Ga’.

On consideration of facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record the learned Assistant Judge decreed the suit.

Being aggrieved by above judgment and decree of the trial Court above defendants as appellants preferred Other Appeal No.189 of 2006 to the District Judge, Netrakona which was heard by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court who dismissed above appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with above judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below above appellants as petitioners moved to this Court with this civil revisional application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil procedure and obtained this Rule.

Mr. Golam Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the father of the plaintiff namely Janab Ali gave oral permission to the defendant No.1 erect a dwelling house but the plaintiff could not prove above claim by legal evidence. Nor the plaintiffs have succeeded to prove that they filed above suit within the statutory period of limitation. But the learned Judges of the Courts below have failed to appreciate above basic deficiency in the suit of the plaintiffs and most illegally the trial Court decreed the suit and the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below without an independent assessment of materials on record dismissed the appeal and upheld the flawed judgment and decree of the trial Court which is not tenable in law.

Mr. Shishir Kanti Majumder, learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos.1-11 submits that admittedly disputed property belonged to Bhupendra Chakrabarty and in his name S.A. Khatian Nos.129 and 132 were correctly recorded and Bhupendra Chakrabarty transferred above land to the predecessor of plaintiff No.1-9 Janab Hossain and after his demise plaintiffs are in possession of above land. Above Janab Hossain permitted defendant No.1 to erect a dwelling hut in a part of the land for his temporary accommodation and after demise of above Janab Hossain plaintiffs requested above defendant No.1 to remove his hut and hand over vacant possession of the disputed land but he refused to do so. Plaintiffs have succeeded to prove their claim of title and previous possession and giving of permission to defendant No.1 to possess a part of above land by mutually corroborative evidence of three competent plaintiff witnesses and production of registered kabala deeds and certified copies of relevant khatians. On consideration of above facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record the learned Judges of both the Courts below rightly and concurrently held that the plaintiffs have succeeded to prove their title and the fact of giving oral permission to defendant Nos.1 to possess a part of the disputed land and accordingly decreed the suit and dismissed the appeal respectively and in the absence of any allegation of non consideration or misreading of any evidence on record this Court cannot in its revisional jurisdiction interfere with above concurrent findings of fact.

I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the respective parties and carefully examined all materials including the pleadings, judgments of the Courts below and evidence on record.

At the very outset the learned Judges of both the Courts below have treated this suit as one under Section 8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 for declaration of title and recovery of possession of 2.64 decimal land. But in fact this is a suit for mere recovery of possession of above disputed land and the suit falls under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. At Paragraph No.8(Ka) of the plaint while seeking relief the plaintiff has sought a decree for only recovery of possession of above 2.64 acres land on removal of structure of the defendants. No relief has been sought for a decree for declaration of title of the plaintiffs in above land. The learned Judges of both the Courts below committed serious illegality in treating this suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession under Section 8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 which is not tenable in law.

It has been stated at Paragraph No.3 of the plaint that above Jaban Hossain gave oral permission to defendant No.1 for erecting a hut in a part of the disputed land. Since this suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 has been filed after more than 10 years from the entry of the defendant into possession of the disputed land the same was hopelessly barred by limitation.

A suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 is legally maintainable when there is a statement both in the plaint and in the evidence of the PW that the plaintiff was dispossessed by the defendant from the disputed land without his consent. In the plaint and in the evidence of PW1 there is no such claim that defendant No.1 entered into the possession of the disputed land without consent of Jaban Hossain. On the contrary it has been stated that defendant No.1 was inducted into possession of the disputed land willingly and with consent of above Jaban Hossain. As such this suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 was misconceived and not tenable in law.

It turns out from certified copy of S.A. Khatian No.132 marked as Exhibit Nos. 4(Kha) that land of above khatian was recorded jointly and in equal shares of two brothers namely Bhupendra Chakrabarty and Purno Chandra Chakrabarty. The plaintiffs claim to have purchased land from Bhupendra Chakrabarty who had 8 anas share in above khatian but on the basis of above purchase the plaintiffs have claimed total land of above khatian No.132. There is no explanation either in the plaint or in the evidence of the PW1 that at any point of time Bhupendra Chakrabarty acquired the land of Purno Chandra Chakrabarty. As such there is no legal basis of plaintiff’s claim of total land of S.A. Khatian No.132 on the basis of purchase of share of Bhupendra Chandra Chakrabarty.

In above view of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record I hold that the learned Judges of both the Courts below totally failed to appreciate the facts and circumstances of the case and relevant laws properly and learned Joint District Judge most illegally dismissed the appeal and affirmed the unlawful and flawed judgment and decree of the trial Court which is not tenable in law.

The learned Advocate for the petitioner lastly submits that the plaint of this suit was defectively drafted and appropriate evidence was not adduce at trial and above deficiencies were caused due to lack of skill and professional experience of the appointed Advocate of the plaintiffs at trial Court. The plaintiffs who are village people should not be made to suffer for above errors and mistakes committed by their appointed Advocate and this suit may be remanded to the trial Court for retrial after giving both parties an opportunity to amend their respective pleadings and adduce further evidence.

Since this was a suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 for mere recovery of possession the plaintiffs be at liberty if so advised to file a regular title suit in an appropriate Court of law.

On consideration of above facts and circumstances of the case and materials on record I find substances in this civil revisional application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Rule issued in this connection deserves to be made absolute.

In the result, the Rule is hereby made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 15.07.2009 passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Netrokona in Other Class Appeal No.189 of 2006 and affirming the judgment and decree dated 20.09.2006 passed by the Assistant Judge, Madar, Netrokona in Other Class Suit No.25 of 2004 is set aside and above suit is dismissed on contest against defendant Nos.1 and4 and ex-parte against the rest.

However, there is no order as to costs.

Send down the lower Courts record immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
On an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure this Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 31.01.2023 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Khulna in Title Appeal No.68 of 2017 and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 19.04.2017 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Fultola, Khulan in Title Suit No.11 of 2015 decreed the suit should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

Facts in short are that the opposite party as plaintiff instituted above suit under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 for recovery of possession of 0.05 acres land. It was alleged that the plaintiff was the rightful owner and possessor of above land and she agreed to sale the same to the defendant for a consideration of Taka 1,20,000/- and on receipt of Taka 40,000/- she executed and registered a bainapatra on 03.05.2006. The defendant further paid Taka 30,000/- on 04.06.2006 and again Taka 30,000/- on 10.07.2006 and the plaintiff gave permission to the defendant to construct a dwelling hut in above land. But the defendant did not pay the remaining consideration money nor obtained a sale deed from the plaintiff. The plaintiff asked the defendant to remove above structure and hand over to her the vacant possession of the disputed land in December, 2014 but the defendant refused to do so.

The suit was contested by defendant No.1 by filing a written statement denying all claims and allegations made in the plaint and stating that the plaintiff executed and registered a bainapatra for sale of disputed land to the defendant on receipt of Taka 40,000/- on 03.05.2006 and delivered possession. The defendant asked the plaintiff to receive the remaining consideration money and execute a sale deed. But above land was enlisted as enemy property and recorded in S.A. Khatian No.1 in the name of the Government. As such the plaintiff could not execute and register a sale deed. The defendant was ready to pay remaining Taka 20,000/- get a sale deed executed by the plaintiff.

At trial plaintiff examined 1 witness and documents of the plaintiffs were marked as Exhibit Nos.1-10 and the defendant examined 3 witnesses and documents of the defendant were marked as Exhibit No."Ka" to "Cha".

On consideration of facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record the learned Senior Assistant Judge decreed the suit.

Being aggrieved by above judgment and decree of the trial Court above defendant as appellant preferred Title Appeal No.68 of 2017 to the District Judge, Khulna which was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court who dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with above judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below above appellant as petitioner moved to this Court and obtained this Rule.

Mr. Shasti Sarker, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that admittedly the plaintiff contracted to sale disputed 5 decimal land to the defendant for Taka 1,20,000/- and on receipt of Taka 40,000/- he executed and registered a bainapatra on 03.05.2006. The plaintiff subsequently receipt Taka 60,000/-. The plaintiff’s name was not mutated for the disputed land and above land was recorded in the name of the Government of Bangladesh and enlisted in ‘Ka’ schedule of the Arpito Sampatti Protterpon Ain, 2001 and published in official gazette in 2012 (Exhibit No.Uma). Due to above reasons the plaintiff was unable to execute and register a sale deed for above land. Defendant was always ready to pay remaining Taka 20,000/- and get a sale from the plaintiff but the plaintiff failed to comply with the terms of the registered bainapatra dated 03.05.2006. But the learned Judge of the Court of Appeal below has miserably failed to appreciate above facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record and most illegally dismissed the appeal and affirmed the flawed judgment and decree of the trial Court which is not tenable in law.

Mr. Ahmed Nowshed Jamil, learned Advocate for the opposite party submits the title of the plaintiff in disputed 5 decimal land is admitted by the defendant. As such the plaintiff was not required to seek any relief as to his title. It is also admitted that plaintiff allowed the defendant to erect a hut in the disputed land since he paid some money. But the defendant instead of payment of remaining Taka 20,000/- and getting a sale deed from the plaintiff continued possession in above land disregarding the request of the plaintiff to hand over possession. The possession of the defendant in above land became unauthorized in December, 2014 and within the statutory period of time the plaintiff has filed this suit on 15.01.2015. On consideration of above facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record the learned Judges of both the Courts below concurrently found that the defendant is an unlawful occupier in the disputed land and rightly decreed the suit and dismissed the appeal respectively which calls for no interference.

I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the respective parties and carefully examined all materials including the pleading, judgments of the Courts below and evidence on record.

It is admitted that the plaintiff was the owner of possessor of disputed 5 decimals land on receipt of Taka 40,000/- and she executed and registered a bainapatra on 05.03.1984 for sale of above land to the defendant for a consideration of Taka 1,20,000/- and delivered possession. On 04.06.2006 and 10.07.2006 the plaintiff admittedly received Taka 60,000/- out of the remaining consideration money.

Admittedly the plaintiff inducted the defendant into the possession of above land willingly and also gave consent to construct a dwelling hut. The plaintiff did not mention in the plaint or in her evidence as PW1 the date when she handed over possession of the disputed land to the defendant. PW1 admitted that she delivered possession to the defendant due to partial payment of the consideration money and the defendant paid Taka 40,000/- on 10.07.2006.

Learned Advocate for the petitioner strenuously submits that this is a suit under Section 8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 but erroneously no relief was sought as to title of disputed 5 decimal land.

Admittedly the only relief sought in this suit was recovery of possession of above 5 decimal land after demolishing the dwelling hut of the defendant. The Specific Relief Act, 1877 provides two separate provisions in Sections 8 and 9 for recovery of possession of immovable property. When a decree for recovery of possession is sought on determination of title or a relief as to declaration or determination of title is sought with the recovery of possession in the plaint then the suit falls under Section 8 of above Act but if in the plaint the sole relief is recovery of possession then that suit falls under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. As mentioned above in this suit plaintiff has sought a decree for recovery of possession.

The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that in December, 2014 the plaintiff asked the defendant to remove her hut from the disputed land and hand over vacant possession to the plaintiff. But she did not comply with above request and from above date the possession of the defendant became unlawful.

Section 8 or Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 deals with the facts of previous possession and the subsequent date of dispossession of the plaintiff from the disputed land and not with the date of request of the plaintiff to hand over possession of above land. Admittedly the date of entry into the possession of the defendant in disputed 5 decimal land was 10.07.2006. This suit has not filed within six months from above date of entry of the defendant in the possession of the disputed land.

There is no claim in the plaint or in the evidence of any PW that that the defendant entered into possession of above land “without the consent” of the plaintiff. No suit for recovery of possession under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 is legally tenable unless the plaintiff claims that the defendant entered into possession of the disputed land without his consent.

While giving evidence as DW1 the defendant produced the Government Gazette Notification dated 1705.2012 which shows that the disputed land was enlisted in ‘Ka’ schedule of the Arpito Samptti Protterpon Ain, 2012. It was further stated by DW1 that he requested the plaintiff to receive remaining Taka 20,000/- and execute and register a kabala deed. But the plaintiff could not do that since the disputed property was enlisted as enemy property and name of the plaintiff was not mutated for above land.

While giving evidence as PW1 the plaintiff has admitted in her cross examination that her name was not mutated for the disputed land in 2006.

The learned Judges of both the Courts below miserably failed to realize that since the defendant got possession pursuant to a contract of sale of above land and the plaintiff had latches in not executing a sale deed and above possession of the defendant was protected by Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The defendant was entitled to continue possession in above land until above admitted registered bainapatra for sale was cancelled by a competent Court on the findings that the defendant failed to perform his obligation under above bainapatra.

In above view of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record I find substance in this revisional application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the Rule issued in this connection deserves to be made absolute.

In the result, the Rule is hereby made absolute.

The impugned judgment and decree dated 31.01.2023 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Khulna in Title Appeal

No.68 of 2017 affirming the judgment and decree dated 19.04.2017 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Fultola, Khulan in Title Suit No.11 of 215 is set aside. Above suit is dismissed on contest with cost.

However, there is no order as to costs.

Send down the lower Courts record immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan J. This Civil appeal by leave granting order dated 31.05.2015 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No .2306 of 2010 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 09.03.2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2910 of 2003 making the Rule absolute reversing the judgment and decree dated 07.04.2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge 1st Court, Narayanganj Civil Appeal No.132 of 2001 allowing the appeal upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated 29.07.2001 passed 4th the learned Senior Assistant judge, 4tn Court, Narayanganj in Civil Suit No.206 of 2000 decreeing the suit.
 
2. The relevant facts necessary for the disposal of this civil appeal are that the respondent No.1 as plaintiff filed Civil suit No.159 of 1999 in the Court of Senior Assistant judge, Rupgonj, Narayanganj against the appellant and pro-forma respondent No.2 along with two others as defendants for declaration of suit title in the `ka' schedule land and also for declaration of `kha' schedule deed as appended to the plain null and void and not binding upon the plaintiff. Subsequently, the said suit was transferred to the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 4th Court Narayanganj and was renumbered as civil Suit No.206 of 2000. The case of the plaintiff, in a nutshell, is that that defendant No.2 was the owner of the suit land and while she was in possession of the suit land, sold the same to the plaintiff on 28.01.1999 through a registered Sqf kabala Deed No.749 at a consideration of Tk. 80,000.00 and also handed over possession of the same in his favour. 

3. Upon purchase of the said land the plaintiff mutated his name in the record of right and paid rent to the authority. The plaintiff gave fencing and cultivated the suit land. The plaintiff while in exclusive possession and enjoyment of the said land, the defendant No.1 by misguiding the defendant No.2, got sale deed executed in his favour and in order to defeat the transfer of the suit land by the defendant No.2 to the plaintiff by sale deed 29.01.1999. The sale deed executed in favour of the defendant No.1 was not only antedated showing execution on 10.12.1998, but in the body of the same a statement to the effect that a Bainanama was executed by the defendant No.2 in favour of the defendant No. 1 on 31.12.1997 was also incorporated though in such a transaction in between mother and son no Bainanama is at all necessary and further the above sale deed was registered on 03.03.1999 after about three months on commission. The defendant No.1 attempted to cancel the mutation of the plaintiff's name in the record of right, kept in the office of the defendant No.4 the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Rupgonj. The plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of his title in the suit land and also for a declaration that the a Sale Deed No.2192 dated 03.03.1999 allegedly exe-cuted by the defendant No.2 in favour of the defendant No.1, is forged, concocted and accordingly illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff. 

4. The defendants No.1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia that the defendant No.2 having been the owner and in possession of the suit land and being in need of money proposed to sell the suit land to the defendant No.1, who agreed to that proposal and on discussion , the value of the land was decided at Tk.50,000.00 and on 31.12.1997 a Bainanama was executed between them and a part payment of Tk.20,000.00 was paid on that day and subsequently, on 10.12.1998 the remaining consideration money, i.e. Tk.30,000.00 was paid to the defendant No.2 and the possession of the suit land was handed over to the defendant No. 1. Thereafter, on 03.03.1999 the title deed was registered between the defendants No.1 and 2 and much prior to the registration of the deed of the plaintiff, the Bainanama of the defendants was executed. The defendants claimed for cancellation of the mutation of the plaintiff since the title deed of the defendant No.1 was lawful and legally binding. 

5. During the trail of the case, the trail Court framed 6(six) issues for disposal of the suit. The plaintiff examined three witnesses as P.Ws.1-3 while the defendants No.1 and 2 examined four witnesses as D.Ws.1-4 Both the parties adduced documentary evidence in support of their respective case. 

6. The trail Court on completion of the trail decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 29.07.2001. Being aggrieved by the judgment of the trail Court the defendants No .1 and 2 preferred Civil Appeal No.132 of 2001 before the learned District Judge, Narayanganj and on transfer, the said appeal was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Narayanganj who allowed the same by judgment and decree dated 07.04.2003 reversing the judgment of the trail Court. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed Civil Revision No .2910 of 2003 before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree dated 07.04.2003 passed by the appellate court and Rule was issued. Upon final hearing, the High Court Division was pleased to make Rule absolute by judgment and decree dated 29.07.2001 

7. Being disgruntled with the judgment and decree dated 29.07.2001 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2910 of 2003 the defendant No.1 preferred the Civil Petition for Leave to appeal No.2306 of 2010 before this Division and after hearing, this Division was pleased to grant leave on 31.05.2015 and hence the instant appeal. 

8. Mr. Nurul Amin, the learned senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant taking us through the judgment and decree of the High Court Division dated 09.03.2010 passed in Civil Revision No.2910 of 2003, judgments and decree of the appellate Court as well as the trail Court, the other materials on record, contends that the High Court Division has committed illegality in totally misconceiving the case of the appellant upon misreading and misconstruing the evidence and materials on record and thereby misdirected beyond the law and facts of the case in passing the erroneous judgment making the Rule absolute occasioning serious miscarriage of justice and as such the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside .The learned senior Counsel contends further that no specific boundary of the suit land had been mentioned in the plaint which is contrary to the provision of Order VII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 but the High Court Division committed serious mistake in holding that in a suit for declaration of title, the description of the land was not so material for adjudication . The learned senior Counsel argues further that in a suit for declaration of title, the plaintiff must prove his exclusive possession in the suit land, while in the case in hand the P.Ws. admitted the possession of the defendants, but the High Court Division without considering said aspect made the Rule absolute. The learned senior Counsel submits further that the defendant No.2 admitted in the written statement that the deed of the defendant No.1 is earlier in point of time compared to the deed of the plaintiff and the plaintiff never denied the contents of the written statement filed by the defendant No.2 but the High Court Division erred in ignoring the said matter and misinterpreting the provisions of Section 47 of the Registration Act. The learned senior Counsel contends, in fine, that although the trail Court famed issue regarding possession, but nowhere within the four corners of the judgment of the trail Court there exists any finding as to the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land, thus, the High Court Division erred in law in not appreciating the aforesaid flaw of the trail Court and as such the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. 

9. Per contra, Mr. A.F Hasan Ariff, the learned senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents argues that P.W.1 deposed supporting the case of the plaintiff particularly the execution of sale deed dated 28.01.1999 and P.Ws.2 and 3 are the attesting witnesses of the said sale deed and all the P.Ws deposed corroborating each other in respect of title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land and the trail Court most legally decreed the suit and the High Court Division on proper scrutiny restored the judgment and decree of the trail Court and as such no interference by this Division with the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is needed and hence the instant appeal is liable to be dismissed. The learned senior Counsel argues next that the defendant No.2 never appeared in the trail court to prove her claim made in the written statement, but the appellate Court could not appreciate the said aspect and most illegally set aside the judgment of the trail Court. The learned senior counsel lastly craves for dismissal of the appeal. 

10. We have perused the judgment and decree dated 09.03.2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2910 of 2003. We have also considered the submissions of the learned Counsels for the both sides and gone through the judgments and decree of the appellate Court as well as the trail Court, evidences and other materials on record. 

11. On scrutiny of the record, it transpires that the plaintiff filed the suit praying for declaration of title only in respect of 35 decimal land out of 113 decimal land appertaining to Hal plot No. 682, but no boundary nor even any specification of the suit land had been described in the plaint. Now adverting to the deposition of the witnesses adduced on behalf of the plaintiff it appears that P.W.1 stated in his deposition in the following way: 
“কয়টা দাগের সম্পত্তি নিয়ে মোকদ্দমা বিবাদী নুর মোহাম্মদকে চিনি। নালিশা ভুমি মধ্যে ৬৮২ দাগে বাড়ি ভুমি। এর মধ্যে জায়গা ৩ পাখি ৮৭ শতাংশ। এর মধ্যে নুর মোহাম্মদের বাড়ি ঘর আছে। দাগে মোট জমি হলো ৩৮৭। সমলা পায় ১১৩, সে এর থেকে ৩৫ রেখেছে। এটা নুর মোহাম্মদের বসত বাড়িসহ কিনা বলতে পারি না।..... আমি এর আগে যে চৌহদ্দির কথা বলেছি সেটা ১১���, ৩৮৭ও নুর মোহাম্মদের চৌহদ্দি, ৩৮৭ এর মধ্যে কয়টা টুকরা বলতে পারি না। সমলা ৩৫ রেখেছে। উত্তরে কে জানি না। দক্ষিণে, পূর্ব পশ্চিমে ও বলতে পারি না"

12. P.W.2 also stated in his cross-examination in the following manner:
"নালিশা জমির দাগ নম্বর জানি না"

13. Again, P.W.3 stated in his cross-examination in the following way: 
"৩৫ শতাংশ জমি, কয়েক দাগেই মিলে কোন দাগে কতটুকু জানি না। ৫১৭ দাগ আছে। সব দাগ নম্বর বলতে পারি না। কোন দাগে কতটুকু বলতে পারি না।"

14. From the above it is clear that none of the P.Ws.1-3 could not state the specific boundary of the suit land which is contrary to the provision of Order VII Rule 3 of the Code Of Civil Procedure,1908 (shortly CPC, 1908). Order VII Rule 3 of CPC, 1908 is extracted below: 
"3. Where the subject matter of the suit is immovable property, the plaint shall contain a description of the property sufficient to identify it, and, in case such property can be identified by boundaries or numbers in a record of settlement of survey, the plaint shall specify such boundaries or numbers." 

15. In view of the aforesaid provisions of law it is evident that the suit for declaration of title without describing the specific boundary is not maintainable in the eye of law. 

16. In this regard , reliance may be placed on the case of Tayeb Ali us Abdul Khaleque , reported in 43 DLR (AD) 87 where it is has been held that the suit being one for declaration of title to an unspecified share of an undivided plot of land is not maintainable without prayer for partition. 

17. It has also been held by this Division in the case of Kanchan Mallik and others us. Saleha Begum and others reported in 9 ALR (AD) 2017 (1) 117 that since the plaint dose not properly identify the suit land and no boundaries are mentioned in the schedule to the plaint nor any sketch map appended thereto which might assist in identifying the suit land, there is no alternative but for parties to establish their respective claim in a suit for partition. Suit for declaration of title is not maintainable.  

18. At this juncture, let us examine whether the plaintiff has been able to prove his possession in the suit land. On perusal of the record it divulges that the plaintiff claims in the plaint that plaintiff acquired the suit land by sale deed dated 27.01.1999 and the possession of the same had been handed over to him on aforesaid date. 

19. P.W.1 stated in his cross examination that "আমি দলিল সম্পাদন, রেজিস্ট্রির সময় ও কথাবার্তার সময় ছিলাম না" But subsequently P.W.1 self contradictorily stated that "যে দিন রেজিস্ট্রি হয় সে দিন দখল দেয়।”

20. Again, P.W.2 stated in her cross-examination that "দখলের সময় ছিলাম না।" 

21. Although P.W.3 sated in his deposition that the possession of the suit land was handed over to the plaintiff, but he could not categorically state on which date the possession was handed over to the plaintiff. Thus, P.Ws.1-3 could not categorically prove the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. 

22. Apart from this, on going through the Exhibit—A it is seen that the Assistant Commissioner of Land, Rupgonj, Narayangonj on the basis of actual physical possession of the suit land by the defendant No.1 set aside the mutation of the plaintiff in the suit land. In the afore-said backdrop, it is squarely proved that the plaintiff has no possession in the suit land. 

23. Moreover, P. W.1 is the attorney of the plaintiff and the plaintiff himself was not examined as witness. On the other hand, P.W.1 failed to prove the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. Although, P.W.2 is the sister of the defendant No 1 she admitted in her cross—examination that she had no good relation with the defendant No.1 P.W.3 is the husband of the P.W.2, Therefore, both P.Ws.2 and 3 are interested witnesses and the plaintiff had not been able to prove his claim by producing any neutral witness. 

24. On contrary, the defendants No.1 and 2 claimed that the defendant No.2 in need of money proposed to sell the suit land to the defendant No,1 who agreed to that proposal and the value of the land was decided at Tk. 50,000.00 and on 31.12.1997 a Bainanama was executed between them and part payment of Tk. 20,000.00 was paid on that day and subsequently, on 10.12.1998 the remaining consideration money, i.e Tk. 30,000.00 was paid to the defendant No.2 and the possession of the suit land was handed over to the defendant No.1 Thereafter, on 03.03.1999 the title deed was registered between the defendants No.1 and 2. To prove the aforesaid claim the defendants No.1-2 examined four witnesses as D.Ws.1-4. out of them D.W.1 is the defendant No.1 himself, D.Ws.2 and 3 deposed in support of possession of the defendant No .1 in the suit land and D.W.4 is the scribe, who deposed establishing the fact of execution of the Bainanama as well as the sale deed dated 03.03.1999. All the D.ws. deposed corroborating each other. Therefore, the defendant No.1 had been able to prove his title and possession in the suit land. 

25. Apart from the above, on going through the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division it appears that the High Court Division reversed the judgment and decree of the appellate court without controverting the findings and observation made by the appellate court. It is settled law that the appellate Court is the last Court of facts and in revisional jurisdiction, the High Court Division can only exercise its power if there is misreading and non-reading of evidence occasioning failure of justice. But the High Court Division while passing the impugned judgment could not show any lawful ground for its interference with the judgment of the appellate Court. In view of the aforesaid reasons, the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court division warrants interference by this Division. Therefore, we find merit in the submissions of the learned senior Counsel for the appellant. In the prevailing circumstances, the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division cannot stand at all in the eye of law. 

26. Accordingly, the instant civil appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. 

27. The judgment and decree dated 09.03.2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2910 of 2003 is hereby set aside. 

End.

full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan J. This Civil Appeal by leave granting order dated 02.06.2014 in Civil Review Petition No.135 of 2010 is directed against the order dated 09.11.2008 passed by this Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1499 of 2007 dismissing the civil petition affirming the judgment and decree dated 09.11.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3747 of 2002 making the Rule absolute reversing the judgment and decree dated 24.04.2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Munshiganj in Civil Appeal No.163 of 2000 dismissing the appeal upon affirming the judgment and decree dated 29.04.1993 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sreenagar, Munshiganj in Title Suit No.07 of 1990 decreeing the suit. 

2. The relevant facts necessary for the disposal of this civil appeal are that the appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.07 of 1990 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sreenagor, Munshigonj praying for declaration of title and permanent injunction over the schedule land as appended to the plaint. The plaintiffs case, in brief, is that 8 annas share of the property measuring .26 acres appertaining to plot No.3123 under C.S. Khatian No.1588 was recorded in the name of Satish Chandra and Roshik Chandra Barori in equal share and the rest 8 annas share measuring .27 acres was recorded in Khatians No.1590-1595 in the name of Altaf Uddin Kazi and others and as per family amicable settlement said Satish Chandra and Roshik Chandra Barori got northern part of the property in plot No.3123 while said Altaf Uddin Kazi and others got southern part of the property. Said Roshik Chandra Barori died leaving Jogesh as one son while Satish Chandra died leaving Haripod as one son. Jogesh used to possess .26 acres of land by family amicable settlement. During the S.A. survey although 8 annas share of the property belonging to Altaf Uddin Kazi and others had been recorded in the name of Zebunnessa and others in S.A. Khatian No.1090, the suit land measuring .26 acres belonging to Jogesh, instead of recording in his name wrongly recorded in the name of the government in Khas Khatian No. 1 . Said Jogesh transferred the suit land to his wife Shova Rani Devi by way of Gift Deed dated 28.03.1978. Subsequently, said Shova Rani Devi transferred the suit land by sale deed dated 23.09.1981. The plaintiff has been possessing the suit land for more than 12 years. The record of the suit land in Khas Khatian No.1 in the name of the government created doubt on the title and possession of the plaintiff and hence the plaintiff instituted the suit. 

3. The government-defendants No.1-5 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the C.S. recorded owners of the suit land left the country before partition and accordingly the suit land was vested in the name of the government and as such rightly recorded in Khas Khatian No.1 and hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

4. The plaintiff examined five witnesses as P.Ws.1-5 while the defendants examined one witness as D. W.1. The documents adduced by the plaintiff had been marked as Exhibits-1-4. On the other hand, the defendants No.1-5 did not adduce any documentary evidence. 

5. The trial Court on completion of the trial decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 29.04.1993. Being aggrieved with the judgment of the trial Court the defendants No.1-5 preferred Title Appeal No.163 of 2000 before the learned District Judge, Munshigonj and the said appeal was eventually transferred to the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Munshigonj, who upon hearing dismissed the same by judgment and decree dated 24.04.2002 and thereby upheld the judgment of the trial Court. Thereafter, the government filed Civil Revision No.3747 of 2002 before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree dated 24.04.2002 passed by the appellate court and Rule was issued. 

6. Upon final hearing, the High Court Division was pleased to make the Rule absolute by judgment and decree dated 09.11.2006 setting aside the judgments and decrees of the appellate Court as well as trial Court and dismissed the suit declaring the suit land as vested property since the original owners had left the country in 1965. 

7. Being disgruntled with the judgment and order dated 09.11.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3747 of 2002 the plaintiff preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1499 of 2007 before this Division and upon hearing the said Civil Petition was dismissed by a judgment and order dated 09.11.2008. 

8. Being dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 09.11.2008 .passed by this Division the plaintiff-appellant filed Civil Review Petition No.135 of 2010 before this Division and upon hearing leave was granted on 02.06.2014 and hence the instant appeal. In Civil Review Petition No.135 of 2010 the leave was granted by this Division to consider the following grounds: 
"I. Because the High Court Division erred in law in making the Rule absolute by not pointing out of misreading, misconstruing and non-consideration of evidence both oral and documentary adduced and produced by the parties which is applicable to interfere in the revisional jurisdiction but the Appellate Division which is the highest Court of the country erroneously affirmed the judgment passed by the High Court Division which deserves for review consideration by this Court. 
III. Because Kabala deeds had been executed and registered in 1981 creates a strong presumption that the registration authority was satisfied that the executant was a valid citizen and national of Bangladesh. The learned Single Judge failed to take into account the legal aspect of the matter and the title was established in Title Suit No. 7 of 1990 decreeing the same in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner and thus fell into a substantial errors and omission on the face of, the record causing a miscarriage of jus-tice which deserves for review consideration by this Court." 

9. Mr. Nikhil Kumar Saha, the learned senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant taking us through the judgment and decree dated 09.11.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3747 of 2002, judgments and decrees of the appellate Court as well as trial Court, the other materials on record, contends that the High Court Division has committed illegality in totally misconceiving the case of the appellant upon mis-reading and misconstruing the evidence and materials on record and thereby mis-directed beyond the law and facts of the case in passing the erroneous judgment occasioning serious miscarriage of justice and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. The learned senior Counsel contends further that the High Court Division erred in law in not taking into account of the fact that Kabala deeds had been executed and registered in 1981 creates a strong presumption that the registration authority was satisfied that the executant was a valid citizen and national of Bangladesh, but the High Court Division did neither advert nor reverse the concurrent findings of the trial Court as well as appellate Court below in this regard and as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside. 

10. In opposition, Mr. Md. Taherul Islam, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents No.1-2 vehemently opposes the submissions put forward on behalf of the appellant. The learned Counsel contends that the High Court Division as revisional Court has exercised its jurisdiction and on proper assessment of the record set aside the judgments and orders of the Courts below. The learned Counsel lastly craves for dismissal of the instant appeal. 

11. We have perused the judgment and order dated 09.11.2006 passed in Civil Revision No.3747 of 2002. We have also considered the submissions of the learned Counsel for the both sides and gone through the judgments and decrees of the appellate Court as well as the trial Court, evidences and other materials on record. 

12. On examination of the record it appears that although the trial Court made some adverse comments as to the plaintiffs claim regarding gift of the suit land to Shova Rani Devi by her husband Jogesh in the year 1978 due to not mentioning of Khatian and Plot number in the said Gift Deed, it categorically found that Jogesh was the owner of the suit land and Shova Rani Devi was his wife and the title regarding the suit land was passed to the plaintiff from Shova Rani Devi by virtue of Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

13. Regarding possession the trial Court found in the following way: 
"বাদী পরে সকল সাক্ষী সামঞ্জস্যপূর্ণভাবে বিরো: ভূমিতে বাদী পরে দখল সম্পর্কে সাক্ষ্য দেয়। অপর দিকে বিবাদী পরে একমাত্র সাক্ষী তাহার সাক্ষ্যে বিরো: ভূমি চেনে না এবং কে দখল আছে তাহা বলিতে পারে নাই। সরকার পরে বন্দোবস্ত গ্রহীতাগণ দখল সম্পর্কে সা্য দিতে আসে নাই।"

14. Therefore, the plaintiff has successfully been able to prove her title and possession in the suit land. 

15. The trial Court found that it has been proved from the documents filed by the plaintiff that the recorded tenants, Rashik Chandra and Shatish Chandra each had a son named Jogesh and Haripoda. Subsequently Haripoda died died leaving behind Jogesh and Jogesh died leaving behind his wife Shova Rani Devi. The deed of gift in favour of Shova Rani Devi by Jogesh was made in 1978 which proved the existence of Jogesh and Shova Rani Devi. In the title deeds of the plaintiff Jogesh was made a witness. From the record it is evident that the title deed of the plaintiff was executed in the year 1981. Thus it is crystal clear that Jogesh was present in the country subsequent to the year 1965. Hence, there is no way to treat the suit land as vested property. 

16. The trial Court also found that the suit was filed within six years from the date when her title to the suit land was invaded and as such the suit is not barred by limitation. The trial Court further held on assessment of evidence that the suit was not bad for defect of parties. 

17. On contrary, although the government claimed that the original owners of the suit land left the country during the partition in the year 1965, but the aforesaid claim has not been proved. Even the government did not take any step to produce any documentary evidence to prove its claim. 

18. In the light of the foregoing discussion it is palpably clear that the trial Court on proper scrutiny of the evidence on record decreed the suit and the appellate Court being the last Court of facts on discussing at length concurred with the findings of the trial Court and dismissed the appeal. But the High Court Division without controverting the concurrent findings of the lower Courts below set aside their judgments. 

19. It is on the record that the Title Appeal No.163 of 2000 was filed out of time by 2651 days i.e. after 7 years 4 months and 11 days of the judgment of the trial Court although the suit was decreed on contest. The appellate Court below observed that the prayer for condonation of delay of 2651 days is not acceptable and accordingly found that the appeal was barred by limitation. 

20. It is settled law that the appellate Court is the last Court of facts and in revisional jurisdiction the High Court Division can only exercise its power if there is misreading and non-reading of evidence occasioning failure of justice. But the High Court Division while passing the impugned judgment could not show any lawful ground for its interference with the judgment of the appellate Court. Due to the reasons stated above, the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division warrants interference by this Division. Therefore, we find merit in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant. 

21. In view of the above prevailing circumstances and in the light of the discussion made above, we find that the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division cannot stand at all in the eye of law. 

22. Accordingly, the instant civil appeal is allowed. 

23. The judgment and decree dated 09.11.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3747 of 2002 is set aside. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 10.053006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3150 of 1998)
full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan J. This civil appeal by leave granting order dated 24.07.2008 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.426 of 2007 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 10.05.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3150 of 1998 discharging the Rule affirming the judgment and decree dated 15.01.1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (presently Joint District Judge), 2nd Court, Noakhali in Title Appeal No.155 of 1990 allowing the appeal reversing the judgment and decree dated 30.08.1990 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 2nd Additional Court, Sadar, Noakhali arising out of Title Suit No.326 of 1986 dismissing the suit. 

2. The relevant facts necessary for the disposal of this civil appeal are, in a nutshell, that on 25.07.1986 the predecessor of the respondents No.1(a)-1(g) Md. Rafiquzzaman Bhuiyan as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.326 of 1986 for declaration of title over 'Kha' schedule land as appended to the plaint stating, inter alia, that the land measuring 20.31 acres appertaining to District Survey Khatian No.9 belonged to the predecessor of the plain-tiff and pro-forma defendants namely Md. Anwar Mia, Md. Amzad Mia and Abdul Mozid Mia in eight anas share and one Hemendra Chandra Roy in rest eight anas share. The father of plaintiff named Alhaj Ali Azam acquired 37 decimal land appertaining to plots No.2105, 2106 and 2107 by amicable settlement. There was a cannel in plot No.2106. Subsequent to the District Survey the said cannel was silted up and the plaintiff and pro-forma defendants took possession of the same. The plaintiff had been possessing the suit land from the long time by erecting some huts thereon and renting the same to the pro-forma defendants. There are various plants and vegetables in the vacant land behind the said huts. There is no Haat in the suit land, but during the M.R.R. survey the suit land was wrongly recorded in Khas Khatian No.1 in the name of the government. The government has no right, title and possession in the suit land. The plain-tiff came to know on 01.06.1986 that the Tahsilder would Lease out the suit land, which cast cloud on the tide of plaintiff over the suit land and hence the suit. 

3. The government as defendant No.1 con-tested the said suit by filing written statement, contending, inter alia, that during the District Settlement Survey the suit land was recorded as Zamindarts Hat-Bazar. After the enactment of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 due to abolishing of Zamindari system the suit land had been vested to the government and during the M.R.R. survey the suit land was correctly recorded in the name of government in Khas Khatian No.1. The plaintiffs predecessor and thereafter the plaintiff took lease of the suit land for the years from 1365 to 1376 B.S., from 1379 to 1385 B.S. and from 1373 to 1392 B.S. admitting the suit land as government property. The plaintiff as well as his predecessor had no right, title and possession in the suit land. Abdul Mannan along with others numbering eighteen had been doing business in the land of plots No.2105 and 2106 after taking yearly lease from the government. The suit is barred by limitation. Since the government has right, title and possession in the suit land the plaintiff is not entitled to get relief as prayed for. 

4. The plaintiff examined four witnesses as P.Ws.1-4 while the defendant No.1 adduced one witness as D.W.1. Both the parties produced documentary evidence in support of their respective claim. 

5. The trial Court on completion of the trial dismissed the suit by judgment and decree dated 30.08.1990. Being aggrieved by the judgment of the trial Court the defendant No.1 preferred Title Appeal No.155 of 1990 and on transfer the said appeal was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge (presently Joint District Judge), 2nd Court, Noakhali and allowed by judgment and decree dated 15.01.1996. Thereafter, the defendant No.1 filed Civil Revision No.3150 of 1998 before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree dated 15.01.1996 passed by the appellate Court and Rule was issued. Upon final hearing the High Court Division was pleased to discharge the Rule by judgment and decree dated 10.05.2006. 

6. Being disgruntled with the judgment and decree dated 10.05.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3150 of 1998 the defendant No.1-appellant preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.425 of 2007 before this Division and leave was granted, hence the instant appeal. 

7. Mr. Md. Taherul Islam, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the appellant taking us through the judgment and decree of the High Court Division dated 10.05.2006 passed in Civil Revision No.3150 of 1998, judgment and decree of trial Court as well as appellate Court, the other materials on record contends that the High Court Division has committed illegality in totally misconceiving the case of the petitioner upon misreading and misconstruing the evidence and materials on record and thereby misdirected beyond the law and facts of the case in passing the erroneous decision discharging the Rule occasioning serious miscarriage of justice and as such the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. The learned Counsel for the appellant contends next that the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the suit land is the land of Haat belonging to the government and the same is in possession of the government from a long time. Accordingly the suit land was recorded in the name of the government in M.R.R. Khatian. The learned Counsel argues next that the government has been possessing the suit land by giving lease to many persons including the plaintiff, but the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division did not consider the said facts and as such the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division is liable to be scraped. 

8. Per contra, Mr. Probir Neogi, the learned senior Advocate appearing along with Mr. Shishir Kanti Mazumder, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents No.1(a)-1(g) have refuted the arguments adduced by the appellant. The learned Counsels contend that both appellate Court as well as the High Court Division concurrently found that the plaintiff has title in the suit land which according to law cannot be interfered with by this Division. The learned Counsels submit next that the government- the other hand appellant failed to prove that the government Haat is situated on the suit land and the same was leased out at the relevant time. The learned Counsels submit further that the findings of facts arrived by the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division being based on record calls for no interference by this Division and hence the instant appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

9. We have perused the judgment and decree dated 10.05.2006 passed in Civil Revision No.3150 of 1998. We have also considered the submissions of the learned Counsel for both sides and gone through the judgments and decrees of the appellate Court as well as the trial Court, evidences and other materials on record. 

10. At the outset, let us see how the plain-tiff has been able to prove his title in the suit land. The plaintiff claims that the suit land measuring 37 decimal belonged to him through family amicable settlement between him and the pro-forma defendants. On plain reading of D.S. Khatian No.9 (Exhibit-1) and attested copy of M.R.R. Khatian No.1 (Exhibit-A) it transpires that the land of suit plots No.2105, 2106 and 2107 had not been recorded as Bazar. 

11. At this juncture, it is prudent to examine the deposition of the witnesses. The plaintiff had been examined as P.W.1, who stated in his deposition that there was neither Zaminder Haat in the suit land nor sit any local Bazar in the suit land. In the same way, P.Ws.2, 3 and 4 consistently corroborated P.W.1 in this regard. On the other hand, D.W.1 stated in his cross-examination that Zamindar Haat was situated in plot No.2132, but he could not file any document in support of recording the land of plots No.2105, 2106 and 2107 as Bazar. 

12. The defendant No.1 further claims that the government has been possessing the suit land by giving lease to various persons and the father of the plaintiff took lease of the suit land as Zamindar Heat from the year 1365 to 1376 B.S. and thereafter the plaintiff took lease of the same for the years from 1369-1385, 1373-1392 B.S. On scrutiny of the records of Miscellaneous Case No.155/75-76 (Exhibits-C-C(8)) it is evident that no plot number was mentioned in the said case and for the said reason it is not proved that the suit land was given lease to the plaintiff. Again, on perusal of Register No.6 (Exhibit-D) of the concerned Union Bhumi Office it is seen that no plot number was mentioned in the relevant pages of the register although some plot numbers had been written in a different colour ink of the pen on the relevant pages of lease of the year 1375, 1379, 1384 and 1394 B.S. and no lease was given at all from 1380 to 1382 B.S. D.W.1 also admitted in his cross-examination that plots No.2105 and 2107 had been written in a different colour ink of the pen. In view of the discussion made above, it is transparent that neither the plaintiff nor his predecessor took lease of the suit land from the government and as such the suit land does not come within the purview of Bazar. 

13. More so, on perusal of hand-drawn sketch map of Haat-Bazaar (Exhibit-B) it appears that the land of plot No.2108 along with other plots situated within the boundary of Bazar has been mentioned as private-owned land. Therefore, the land of suit plots contiguous to Bazar is also naturally private land in which the plaintiff has title and possession. On the other hand, the defendant No.1 also could show the suit land was acquired by the government and awarded compensation to the original owner. 

14. Although the defendant No.1 claims that the government gave lease of the suit land to Abdul Mannan and some others, but the defendant No.1 could not produce any document in support of the said lease. Moreover, none of the lessees deposed before the Court to prove the claim. 

15. Regarding possession, the plaintiff examined four witnesses including himself. P.W.1 deposed that he is in possession of the suit land. P.Ws.2, 3 and 4 also deposed supporting the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. 

16. In the light of the foregoing discussion, the trial Court without proper appraisal of the oral evidence as well as documentary evidence available on the record dismissed the suit. The appellate Court correctly set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and the High court Division lawfully upheld the judgment and decree of the appellate Court. We do not find any perversion in the impugned judgment and decree of the High Court Division and as such we are impelled to hold that the plaintiff has acquired a valid title and possession in the suit land. Due to reasons stated above, it does not warrant interference with the judgment and decree dated 10.05.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3150 of 1998. Therefore, we do not find any merit in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant and as such the instant civil appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

17. Consequently, the instant civil appeal is dismissed. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 23.02.2010 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 632 of 2009)
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique CJ. This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 23.02.2010 passed by this Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 632 of 2009. 

2. The relevant facts, for disposal of this appeal, in short, are that the land measuring an area of 15.20 acres in C.S khatian No. 122, 252, 255 and 817 of Mouja Chalita Bunia under Police Station Morrelganj owned by two brothers namely, Serajuddin and Daliluddin in equal shares. Serajuddin died leaving two sons, the defenant Nos. 13 and 14 and Daliluddin died leaving four sons, the plaintiffs, the defendant No.1 Abdul Gani and Abdul Aziz. Serajuddin and Daliluddin decided to transfer the suit land by way of gift to their sons. At the time the plaintiffs were minors. The suit land was recorded in the names of their two brothers Abdul Aziz and Abdul Gani Daliluddin and Serajuddin eecuted two different transfer deeds on 14m June, 1937 and 30th June, 1937 to their sons in respect of 15.20 acres. On the basis of those deeds, the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 have been possessing their shares. The plaintiffs have been living in different houses. On 5tn September, 1980 Anwar Hossain, defendant No. 2 disclosed that S.A. record-of-rights was not prepared in the plaintiffs' names, which clouded their title in the suit land. Hence, was the suit. 

3. The defendant Nos. 3-6, 8-12, 13-14 and 18-20 contested the suit by filing separate written statements contending, inter alia, that there was no cause of action to file the suit, the suit was not maintainable, the same was barred by limitation and also barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. They denied the claim of the plaintiffs. 

4. Specific case of the defendants was that Daliluddin and Serajuddin transferred a portion of the suit land of C.S. khatian No. 817 to Abdul Aziz, defendant Nos. 1 and 13 to 14 by a sale deed dated 14.06.1937 and gifted the rest land to them from the remaining 3 khatians by a deed of gift dated 30.06.1937. The suit should be dismissed. 

5. The learned Assistant Judge by his judgment and decree dated 29th May, 1990 decreed the suit. Against the said judgment and decree, the appellants and respondent No.3 preferred Title Appeal No. 129 of 1990 and the Appellate Court by the judgment and decree dated 12th September, 1994 allowed the appeal. The plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No. 430 of 1995. The High Court Division made the rule absolute by judgment and order dated 

18.11.2008 and restored those of the trial Court. The defendants then moved this Division in Civil Petition No. 632 of 2009 against the judgment and order of the high Court Division. This Division dismissed the leave petition by a judgment and order dated 23.02.2010. Against the said judgment and order of this Division, the appellants have filed review petition and obtained leave. 

6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants, submits that the plaintiffs sought for declaration of title in respect of 3.80 acres of land out of 15.20 acre in four khatians without giving specific boundary of the said land. He further submits that the suit itself was no maintainable without seeking relief for cancellation of the deeds inasmuch as admittedly, the suit property to defendant No.1, Abdul Aziz, predecessor-in-interest of defendants No.2-12 and the defendants No. 13 and 14 by two separate registered transfer deeds dated 14m and 30m June, 1937 but the plaintiffs did not seek any relief by way of cancellation of those deeds. He further submits that the suit itself was hopelessly barred by limitation, this Division as well as the High Court Division failed to consider the point of limitation thereby, erroneously decreed the suit. 

7. Admittedly, one Daliluddin and Serajuddin were the original owners of the land measuring an area 15.20 acres of C. S khatian No. 122, 252, 255 and 817. Serajuddin died leaving two sons, the defendant No. 13 and 14. On the other hand Daliluddin died leaving behind plaintiffs, defendant No. 1 Abdul Gani and Abdl Aziz, predecessor-in-interest of the defendant No. 2 to 12. The plaintiffs claimed their title in respect of 3.80 acres of land as two sons of Daliluddin. 

8. The plaintiffs claimed title to 3.80 acres of land from CS khatinas no 122, 252, 255 and 817 but the schedule to the plaint describes only the lands of three CS khatians namely CS Khatian no 122, 252 and 255. There is no description of land which they claim from CS khatian no 817. In a suit for declaration of title there shall be proper identification of land as per Order 7 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Neither the courts below nor the High Court Division noticed the above-mentioned anomaly in the schedule of the plaint. The Appellate Court categorically stated that upon perusal of exhibit No. "জ" it appeared that Daliluddin Howlader was literate and he could sign but it appeared from the solenama that Daliluuddin Howlader put his thumb impression there-in which clearly established the fact that Daliluddin Howlader did not compromise the suit with the plaintiffs through solenama. But one of the grounds for setting aside the judgments of the Appellate Court by the High Court Division was the com-promise of the suit by the defendant No 1 and 15 (Daliluddin) with the plaintiff by solanama. The High Court Division did not reverse the findings of the Appellate Court that Daliluddin was literate and, therefore, his thumb impression on the solename made the same highly doubtful. 

9. It is the definite case of the defendants that Daliluddin and Serajuddin earlier executed and registered two transfer deeds dated 14.06.1937 and 30.06.1937 in respect of entire 15.20 acres of land in favour of Abdul Aziz, predecessor-in-interest of the defendants No.2-12, defendant No.1, and defendants No. 13 to 14. The last Court of facts on consideration of the evidence, held, "উভয় পক্ষের দাখিলকৃত দলিলপত্র পর্যালোচনা করলে দেখা যায়, ১৪/৬/৩৭ ও ৩০/৬/৩৭ তারিখের দলিলে সিরাজউদ্দিন ও দলিল উদ্দিন ১, ১৩, ১৪ ও হাল মৃত আঃ আজিজের বরাবরে নালিশী জমি হস্তান্তর করে ছিলেন।" Those two transfer deeds were executed and registered about 42 years before filing the instant suit. The plaintiffs in the plaint, simply prayed for the declaration of title in respect of 3.80 acres, that is, 'Atli share of total land measuring 15.20 acres but they did not seek any relief against those two registered deeds and it is not their case that those two deeds were not acted upon. Since after execution and registration of deeds dated 14.06.1937 and 30.06.1937, the title of entire property measuring 15.20 acres including the suit land had been vested in favour of four sons of Daliluddin and Serajuddin, that is, long before the alleged acquisition of title by these plaintiffs by way of inheritance, we are of the view that the plaintiffs, who claimed title in the suit land by way of inheritance, did not acquire any title in the same. 

10. In such view, we find substance in the appeal. 

11. Thus, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order passed by this Division under the review is set aside and judgment and order dated 18.11.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 430 of 1995 is also set aside. 

End.

full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 02.03.2021 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3112 of 2017 making the Rule absolute by setting-aside the judgment and order of the first revisional court as well as the judgment and order of the trial Court. 

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the civil petition are that the petitioners herein as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.375 of 1975 in the Court of learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Moulvibazar, for declaration of title in respect of the suit schedule land, con-tending interalia, the Government settled the said land to South Sylhet Supply Society Limited through patta; Subsequently the suit land was sold in auction for arrear rent in a rent execution case which was purchased by Khirod Bihari Dev Chowdhury on 19.07.1951 and the sale certificate was obtained on 24.11.1951; Said Khirod Bihari Dev Chowdhury sold the land to the plaintiffs vide two registered deeds dated 15.04.1969; After purchase, plaintiffs filled up the suit land and constructed a petrol pump thereon after taking necessary permission from the authority concerned; The suit land has been wrongly recorded in the name of the Government; Hence, the suit. 

3. Defendant contested the suit by filing written objection denying the material allegations made in the plaint, stating interalia, that the suit is not maintainable and barred by limitation and there is no cause of action. 

4. After hearing the parties, the learned Munsif decreed the suit. 

5. Being aggrieved, the defendant preferred Title Appeal No.58 of 1981 in the Court of learned District Judge, Sylhet, and on transfer the Appeal heard and disposed of by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Moulvibazar, who upon hearing allowed the appeal vide judgment and order dated 22.05.1985 and thereby set-aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

6. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff-opposite parties preferred Civil Revision No.02 of 1985 under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the High Court Division. 

7. Upon hearing, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute and sent the case back on remand vide judgment and order dated 04.11.2021 for re-trial. 

8. As per order of the High Court Division, trial of the case was going on and during the trial the plaintiffs filed an application under order-VI rule 17 of the code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the plaint in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Moulvibazar. Defendant Nos.1 and 2 filed written objection against the application for amendment. 

9. After hearing learned senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Moulvibazar, allowed the application for amendment vide order dated 09.06.2014. 

10. The defendant as petitioner filed revisional application under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of learned District Judge, Moulvibazar, who after hearing the parties disallowed the revision vide judgment and order dated 09.02.2017. 

11. Having aggrieved and dissatisfied, the defendant No.02 as petitioner filed Civil Revision No.3112 of 2017 before the High Court Division under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

12. After Hearing the parties, a Single Bench of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute and thereby set aside the judgment and order of the first revisional court as well as order of the trial Court. 

13. Feeling aggrieved, the plaintiffs as petitioners preferred instant civil petition for leave to appeal invoking Article 103 of the Constitution. 

14. Mr. Nurul Amin, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the High Court Division passed the remand order in Civil Revision No.02 of 1085 for re-trial of the suit alongwith a direction to identify the suit land and exact location and the amendment application was filed providing some more description of the suit land as such the proposed amendments are in no way inconsistent with the remand order of the High Court Division and thus, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. He also submits that the plaintiffs sought the amendment to bring all the disputed facts in the suit for proper adjudication of all disputes between the parties and the identity of the suit land has an important role for fair justice between the parties and in that view of the matter the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. 

15. No one appears for the respondents. 

16. Heard the learned Advocate for the petitioners. We have gone through the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division as well as the other papers/documents contained in the paper book. 

17. It appears that the High Court Division sent the case back on remand for retrial vide judgment and order dated 04.11.2002 in Civil Revision No.02 of 1985. It also appears that the plaintiffs filed application for amendment of the plaint under Order-VI Rule-17 praying to insert two facts in the plaint regarding R.S. Khatian and a decree passed in the Title Appeal No.130 of 1992. Plaintiffs filed the suit in 1975 and R.S. survey started to operate in the area from around 1990. So both the facts argued by the plaintiffs were subsequent development to the institution of the suit and in no way change the nature and character of the suit for declaration of title. 

18. This Division in the case of Khaledur Reza vs. Saleha Begum, reported in 2 BLC (AD) 20, held that a plaint may be amended with the changed circumstances as well as in the case of Sultan Ahmed vs. Poran Chandra, reported in 28 DLR 130, it was held that where the amendment does not alter the averments of the plaint but is sought to introduce events occurring sub-sequent to filing of the suit may be allowed. 

19. In view of the above, we find sub-stance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. 

20. Accordingly, this civil petition dis-posed of. 

21. The impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3112 of 2017 is hereby set-aside. 

22. However, defendant-respondent No.1 is permitted to file additional written statement if, he so desire. 

23. No order as to costs. 

End.
