full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan J. This Civil Appeal by leave granting order dated 23.02.2017 passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3006 of 2015 is directed against the judgment and order dated 03.09.2015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3916 of 2013 making the Rule absolute remanding the suit to the trial Court for holding trial de novo in the light of the observation made in the judgment upon reversing the judgment and decree dated 25.09.2013 passed by the learned District Judge, Rangamati in Civil Appeal No.56 of 2012 dismissing the appeal affirming the judgment and decree dated 22.03.2012 passed by the Court of Joint District Judge, Rangamati in Civil Suit No.238 of 2011 decreeing the suit. 

2. The relevant facts necessary for the disposal of this Civil Appeal are that the appellant as plaintiff instituted Civil Suit No.238 of 2011 impleading the respondents as defendants for a declaration of title in the suit land and also for declaration of Power of Attorney executed by the defendant No.1 being null and void not binding upon the plaintiff also for cancellation of Settlement Case No.01/2005-06. The case of the plaintiff, inter alia, is that the plaintiffs mother Mostafa Khatun was the original owner of the suit land measuring 01 acre and she got the suit land in. the year 1971-72 pursuant to Settlement Case No. 23(D) of 1971-72 and took over possession of the suit land and paid rent there-of. The government declared the suit land along with its adjacent land as Khas land for establishment of Parjatan Corporation in the year 1982. After establishment of Parjatan Corporation 8.53 acres of land was found in excess which was vested in the Bazar Fund Administration and the same was kept out of the Parjatan Corporation area. Thereafter, a decision was taken for resettlement of the said excess land amongst the affected persons and accordingly 30 decimal of land instead of 1.00 acre was given settlement in the name of the plaintiffs mother Mostafa Khatun. The plaintiff and his mother went to the concerned office and filed their objection, but did not get any relief. Meanwhile all settlement process in respect of the land of Hill. Districts stopped in the year 1986. The plaintiffs mother Mostafa Khatun died on 01.06.1984 leaving the plaintiff and one daughter defendant No.2. After the death of the plaintiffs mother, the plaintiff and the defendant No2 had been residing in the suit land with their family members. The defendant No.1 is the son of the defendant No.2 and he created a false Power of Attorney in respect of the suit land to grab the same. The defendant No.1 filed Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1984 before the Deputy Commissioner and thereafter filed Civil Suit No.72 of 2004 claiming that Mostafa Khatun is the grandmother of the defendant No.1 and the suit land is to be recorded in his name in the Bazar Fund Administration. On 10.01.2005 the Deputy Commissioner directed the concerned official to make settlement in favour of the defendant No.1 in respect of 1.00 acre of land on the priority basis if the settlement process starts again. Thereafter, the defendant No.1 filed Review Miscellaneous Case No.05 of 2008 before the Deputy Commissioner and subsequently upon transfer to the learned Joint District Judge the same was renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1984 which was allowed on 25.05.2009 with a direction to record the suit land in the name of the defendant No.1 under the Bazar Fund Tauzi and accordingly the suit land was recorded in the name of the defendant No.1 through Settlement Case No.01/ 2005-06. Mostafa Khatun died on 01.06.1984 and the defendant No.1 created the Power of Attorney beyond the knowledge of the plaintiff by practicing fraud upon the authority and also got recorded his name in respect of the snit land under the Bazar Fund Tauzi which is illegal and void. The defendant No.1 has concocted the said Power of Attorney to deprive the plaintiff and other heirs of Mostafa Khatun. Thus the title of the plaintiff had become clouded and hence the suit. 

3. The defendant No.1respondent No.1 contested the suit filing written statement denying all the material averments made in the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and is barred by limitation. The plaintiff has no right, title, interest and possession on the suit land and the plaintiff has no locus standi to file the suit. The suit land was settled in the name of Mostafa Khatun by Settlement Case No.23 (D) of 1971-72 and the same was declared as Khas land on 08.09.1976 by the Deputy Commissioner and vested to the Bazar Fund Administration. The plaintiffs mother executed and registered a bond being No.146/84-85 on 24.07.1984 in favour of the defendant No.l. The defendant No.1 is entitled to get all legal facilities over the movable or immovable properties of Mostafa Khatun by the registered Power of Attorney and accordingly the plaintiff on 05.08.1984 executed a Nadabi Patra in favour of the defendant No.1, thus the defendant No.1 is entitled to get 1.00 acre of land from the Bazar Fund Administration. Subsequently the defendant No.1 filed Civil Suit No.72 of 2004 and obtained an order to be recorded 1.00 acre of land thereby resumed the settlement process. Later on, he filed Review Misc. Case No.05 of 2008 which was renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No.236 of 2008 and obtained an order directing the Bazar Fund Administration to record his name. The defendant No.1 got the suit land by way of settlement from the Bazar Fund Administration and got his name recorded in the Bazar Fund Tauzi filing Settlement Case No.1/20052006 on 23.06.2009 and since then the defendant No.1 has been possessing the suit land paying rent thereof. The plaintiff did not raise any claim or objection in respect of the suit land even before the Bazar Fund Administration or the concerned Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati Hill District. The land of the plaintiffs predecessor was vested to the Government on 08.09.1976 and as such the plaintiff or his predecessor has no right, title or interest in the suit land. The suit is liable to be dismissed. 

4. Upon final hearing, the trial Court decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 22.03.2012. Being aggrieved by the judgment of the trial Court the defendant No.1 preferred Civil Appeal No.56 of 2012 before the learned District Judge, Rangamati. Having heard the Appeal was dismissed by the judgment and decree dated 25.09.2013. Against the said judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below the defendant No.1 filed Civil Revision No.3916 of 2013 before the High Court Division. On hearing, the High Court Division vide judgment and order dated 03.09.2015 made the Rule absolute in Civil Revision No.3916 of 2013 reversing the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below and remanded the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial in the light of the observations made in the judgment. 

5. Being disgruntled with the judgment and decree dated 03.0912015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3916 of 2013 the plaintiff-appellant preferred the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3006 of 2015 before this Division and after hearing this Division was pleased to grant leave on 23.02.2017 and hence the instant Appeal. 

6. Mr. A.K.M. Fazlul Haque, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant taking us through the judgment and order dated 03.09.2015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3916 of 2013, judgments and decrees of the appellate Court below as well as the trial Court, the other materials on record, contends that the High Court Division has failed to conceive that the Courts below did not commit any illegality in non-examination of any witness in view of the provision of Rules 1 and 2 of the Rules for the Administration of the Chittagong Hill Tracts framed under Section 18 of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulation, 1900. The learned Counsel contends next that the High Court Division has committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice sending the suit on remand to the trial Court established under the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulation, 1900 after treating the same as 'dead law'. The learned Counsel submits next that the High Court Division has failed to conceive that since the defendant-respondent No.1 did not raise any objection against the non-examination of witness in the Courts below, he should be debarred from raising the said question in Civil Revision before the High Court Division. The learned Counsel argues next that the High Court Division has committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment ignoring Section 19 of the said Regulation whereby a Civil Revision is debarred under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against a decision passed, act done or order made under the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulation, 1900 or the Rules thereunder. The learned Counsel contends, in fine, that the High Court Division has committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment without considering the fact that since the Parliament has given validity of the said regulation by way of amending the same, it should not be declared as a 'dead law' while exercising power under Civil Revisional jurisdiction, which does not have any authority of such declaration and as such the impugned judgment and order of the High court Division is liable to set aside. 

7. Per contra, Mr. Md. Golam Mostafa, learned Advocate on behalf of the respondents put forward his submission supporting the judgment and order dated 03.9.2015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3916 of 2013. He contends that the Chittagong Hill-tracts Regulation, 1900 being a dead law, the High Court Division is authorized to exercise its revisional jurisdiction against the judgment of the appellate Court below. The learned Counsel contends next that the averments of plaint and the written statement are not substantive evidence, the plaintiff is to prove his case by adducing sufficient oral and documentary evidence, but the trial Court without examination of any witness relying on some documents which were not admitted as evidence illegally decreed the suit while the High Court Division on appreciating the said aspects most lawfully made the Rule absolute. The learned Counsel for the respondents lastly craves for dismissal of the appeal being the same is devoid of merit. 

8. We have perused the judgment and order dated 03.09.2015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3916 of 2013. We have also considered the submissions of the learned Counsels for both sides and gone through the judgments and decrees of the appellate Court below as well as the trial Court and other materials on record. 

9. On perusal of the impugned judgment and order dated 03.09.2015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3916 of 2013 it transpires that the High Court Division referring the decisions made by the High Court Division in the case of Rangamati Food Products Ltd. Vs. Commissioner of Customs and others reported in 10 BLC 524 and BLAST Vs. Bangladesh reported in 61 DLR 109 observed that the Chittagong Hill-tracts Regulation, 1900 (hereinafter referred as Regulation, 1900) is a dead law and all laws which are in force in Bangladesh are equally applicable to the Hill District of Chattogram, thus the Civil Revision filed by the respondent No.1 before the High Court Division was maintainable.
 
10. Needless to say that the Chittagong Hill-tracts consist of three districts viz. Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban. Now let us examine whether the Regulation, 1900 is an obsolete or dead law. The controversy in this regard has fairly been settled by this Division in the case of Government of Bangladesh Vs. Rangamati Food Products and others reported in 69DLR(AD) (2017)432. Referring the relevant provisions of law of the Regulation, 1900 and other laws vis-a-vis socio-economic and cultural back-ground of the tribal people of the hill-tracts and upon a detailed discussion on the issue this Division observed in the said case as follows: 
"22  On consideration of this provision, this court held in Civil Appeal No. 147 of 2004 that "Therefore, there is no gainsaying that despite setting up of civil courts and criminal courts with the judicial officers, the courts will be guided by the Regulation of 1900 subject to certain variations. Therefore, the government recognizes the Regulation of 1900 by promulgating three Zilla Parishad Ains, one Regional Parishad Ain and by amending the Regulation of 1900. How then can it be accepted the contention that this Regulation of 1900 has no force of law?" 
23. These provisions clearly suggest no inference other than that the Regulation 1 of 1900 has force of law and subsisting. In Civil Appeal No. 147 of 2004, this court concluded its opinion observing that the object of promulgating the Regulation was for the purpose of giving special privilege to the tribal people of the three hill districts and to protect and preserve their culture, traditional practices, customs etc. A custom which is followed in a particular region and recognized by the government has a force of law (article 152 of the constitution). 
24. By amendment of section 7 of the Regulation by the Chittagong Hill Tracts (Amendment) Act, 2003 for the words 'a district' the words 'three districts' have been substituted, the words 'and civil' and 'civil' have been deleted. 
Section 8 (1) has been substituted as under: 
"(1) The Rangamati, Khagrachory and Bandarban districts, of the Chittagong Hill Tracts shall constitute three separate sessions divisions and the concerned District Judge shall be the Sessions Judge of the respective sessions divisions and the Joint District Judge shall be the Assistant Sessions Judge." 
and in sub-section (2) the word 'As' has been substituted for the word 'The' and in the sixth line the word 'warrant' has been deleted. Thereafter subsections (3) (4) and (5) have been in the following manner: 
"(3) The Rangamati, Khagrachori and Bandarban districts of the Chittagong Hill Tracts shall constitute three separate civil jurisdictions under three District fudges. 
(4) The Joint District Judge as a court of original jurisdiction, shall try all civil cases in accordance with the existing laws, customs and usages of the districts concerned, except the cases arising out of the family laws and other customary laws of the tribes of the districts of Rangamati, Khagrachori and Bandarban respectively which shall be triable by the Mauza Headmen and Circle Chiefs. 
(5) An appeal against the order, judgment and decree of the Joint District 'fudge shall lie to the District judge." 
26.......  The three districts have been constituted three separate civil jurisdictions under three District Judges and a Joint District judge has been given power to exercise a court of original jurisdiction under section 8(4). While exercising such power he shall follow the existing laws, customs and usages of the districts concerned, except the cases arising out of Family Laws and other customary laws of the tribes of the districts of Rangamati, Khagrachori and Bandarban respectively, which shall be triable by the Mauza headmen and Circle Chiefs. Against an order, judgment or decree passed by the Joint District, the District Judge have been given the appellate power."  

11. What becomes conspicuous from the above is that by amendment of Section 8 of the Regulation, 1900 by the Chittagong Hill Tracts (Amendment) Act, 2003 Sub-sections (3) (4) and (5) have been added after Sub-section (2). Sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 8 provides that Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban shall constitute three separate civil jurisdictions under three District Judges. The Joint District Judge in each hill district as a court of original jurisdiction shall try all civil cases in accordance with the existing laws, customs and usages of the respective district while the cases arising out of the family laws and other customary laws of the tribes in those districts shall be triable by the Mauza Headmen and Circle Chie. According to Sub-section (5) an appeal against the order, judgment and decree of the Joint District Judge shall lie to the District Judge. 

12. At this juncture, the pertinent question surfaces as to whether the High Court Division shall exercise a Civil Revisional Jurisdiction against the order and judgment of the District Judge of three hill districts. 

13. Section 19 the Regulation, 1900 provides the following: 
"Except as provided in this Regulation or in any other enactment for the time being in force, a decision passed, act done or order made under the Regulation or the rules there under, shall not be called in question in any Civil and Criminal Court." 
 
14. It has been held by this Division in the case of Rangamati Food Products (supra) that-
"27. The High Court Division has been given all appellate powers under the Code of Criminal Procedure under section 9, but in respect of civil disputes no such power has been given upon the High Court Division. These provisions are sufficient to come to the conclusion that the government still recognize the customs and usages of the tribal people of the region while adjudicating civil disputes." 
 
15. In view of the above decision in the case of Rangamati Food Products (supra) and the provisions of the Regulation, 1900 the settled position of law is that unlike other districts of the country the High Court Division has no appellate or revisional jurisdiction as regards civil disputes arising in the Chittagong Hill-tracts viz. Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban. Having considered the reasons stated above, it is our considered view that the Regulation, 1900 is not a dead law in respect of civil disputes arise in the Chittagong Hill-tracts; rather the civil administration of justice is regulated only in accordance with the provisions laid down in the Regulation, 1900. But in the case in hand, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute while exercising its power under revisional jurisdiction which is exercised in violation of the settled law declared by this Division and as such the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be interfered with by this Division. 

16. It transpires from the record that the High Court division while making the Rule absolute remanded the original suit to the concerned trial Court for holding trial de novo giving opportunity to the plaintiff and defendant No.1 to prove their respective case by adducing sufficient oral and documentary evidence. The High Court Division observed that the proposition of law is well settled that the averment of plaint and written statement are not admissible as evidence unless corroborated by other oral as well as documentary evidence. It has been further observed that the plaintiff miserably failed to prove his case without examining any single witness in support of his case and the trial Court decreed the suit on the basis of documents which were not legally admitted into the evidence. 

17. Delving into the issue, we need to have a glimpse of the relevant law in this regard. To supplement the provisions of the Regulation, 1900 Section 18(2)(a) of the said Regulation delegated power to frame relevant Rules as regards the administration of civil justice in the Chittagong Hill-Tracts and other matters stated in the said Section. In pursuant to Section 18 of the Regulation, 1900 Rules for the Administration of the Chittagong Hill Tracts was made by the Government of Bengal in May 1900. Rules 1, 2 and 3 of the Rules for the Administration of the Chittagong Hill Tracts deal with the Administration of Civil Justice. Rules 1, 2 and 3 are extracted in the following: 
"Administration of Civil Justice-
1. The Administration of Civil Justice shall be conducted in the most simple ad expeditious manner compatible with the equitable disposal of the matter or suits. 
2. The officer dealing with the matter or suit will in the first instance endeavour, upon the viva voce examination of the parties to make a justice award between them. Witnesses should not be sent for, except when the officer is unable without them to come to a decision upon the facts of the case. 
3. The record shall contain the following particulars, namely, the name of the plaintiff, the name of the defendant, the nature of the claim or other matter in litigation, an abstract of the plaintiffs case and abstract of the defendant's case, an abstract of the depositions of the witnesses (where witnesses are examined), the ground of the decision, and the order signed and dated " 

18. On perusal of the Rule 1 of the Rules for the Administration of the Chittagong Hill Tracts it is manifest that the administration of civil justice shall be conducted in the most simple ad expeditious manner. Rule 2 lays down that while dealing with the civil suit the officer in the first instance upon oral examination of the parties will endeavour to make a justice award between them and witnesses should not be called for except when the officer is unable without them to come to a decision upon the facts of the case. Rule 3 provides about the contents of a record and the abstracts of the depositions of the witnesses and those are needed only where witnesses are examined as stated in Rule 2. Therefore, regarding the case in hand, our candid view is that the trial Court did not commit any illegality by not examining the witnesses or not requiring the plaintiff and defendant to prove documentary evidence through the witnesses as stipulated in the Evidence Act. 

19. Now let us examine how the trial Court decreed the suit. From the record, it appears that admittedly the original owner of the suit land was Mostafa Khatun. The plaintiff appears to claim that by creating a forged Power of Attorney the defendant No.1 obtained an order for correction of the record in Suit No.236 of 2008 and thereafter without getting any relief in Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1984 the defendant No.1 again with the surreptitious means of using the said Power of Attorney got order of correction of record in his favour in Suit No.72 of 2004 and finally got settlement of the suit land by Settlement Case No.01/05-06. Therefore, the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title in the suit land. 

20. On examination of the record, it is apparent that the original copy of the said Power of Attorney had not been filed by the defendant No.1. Only a photocopy of the said Power of Attorney was filed from which it appears that the names of the witnesses are illegible. Moreover,' the said Power of Attorney being an unregistered instrument is not admissible in the eye of law as per Section 12 of the Regulation. 

21. Again, it is evident from the death certificate of Mostafa Khatun that she died on 01.06.1984 at the age of 80 years while the alleged Power of Attorney was created by the defendant No.1 on 24.07.1984 wherein said Mostafa Khatun had been shown as the executant of the same. But practically it is impossible for Mostafa Khatun to execute the alleged Power of Attorney after her death. Therefore, it is crystal clear that the alleged Power of Attorney which is the basis of title of the defendant No.1 is forged and fabricated one and as such the same does not have any evidentiary value in the eye of law. On the other hand, the plaintiff being the son of the original owner of the suit land acquires title in the suit land by way of succession. 

22. It transpires from the record that the defendant No.1 filed a Nadabipatra dated 05.08.1984 in support of his title. But on going through the said Nadabipatra it divulges that there is no witness in the said document and the discrepancy is patent between the signature of the plaintiff available in the Nadabipatra with the one contained in the plaint. Therefore, it is evident that the said Nadabipatra is forged and fabricated one. In the premises made above, we find that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case and the trial Court on proper appreciation of facts and law decreed the suit while the appellate Court below rightly dismissed the Appeal. 

23. In view of the aforesaid reasons vis-a-vis the detailed discussion regarding the facts and law of the case, we find that the High Court Division committed illegality in making the Rule absolute by the impugned judgment and order dated 03.09.2015 and the same warrants interference by this Division. Therefore, we find merit in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant. In the premises made above, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division cannot stand at all in the eye of law. 

24. Resultantly, the instant Civil Appeal is allowed. 

25. The judgment and order dated 03.09.2015 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3916 of 2013 is hereby set aside. 

End.

full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan CJ. This Civil Appeal by leave granting order dated 01.03.2015 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.762 of 2013 is directed against the judgment and order dated 12.04.2005 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.734 of 2002 discharging the Rule. 

2. The relevant facts necessary for disposal of this Civil Appeal are, in a nut-shell, that the appellant as writ petitioner filed the Writ Petition No.734 of 2002 for a declaration that the judgment and order dated 12.10.1992 passed by the First Court of Settlement in Settlement Case No.22/89(ka-67-1&2, Mirpur, Dhaka) has been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

3. The case of the writ petitioner, in brief, is that the property in question was duly enlisted in the 'Ka' list as abandoned property and the Government was in possession. The writ-respondent No.2 filed a suit in the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka and obtained an ex parte decree on the basis of which they moved the Court of settlement and the said Court illegally passed the judgment and order excluding the property from the list of abandoned property. 

4. The writ-respondent No.2 filed an affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the Writ Petition contending, inter alia, that the property in question originally belonged to the government and one Sk. Majnu vide lease deed dated 21.05.1964 took lease of the same from the government. Subsequently, the writ respondent No.2 acquired the said property from Sk. Majnu by a registered deed dated 26.12.1973. But when she approached to the commissioner of Housing and Settlement for mutation of the said property in her name, her prayer was refused on the ground that she did not obtain prior permission to purchase the house and it was an abandoned property. Having been refused she filed a suit being Title Suit No.393 of 1984 before the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka for declaration that the property is not an abandoned property and also for declaration of title and for direction to mutate the land in her name. The further case of the writ respondent No.2 is that her licensee Sadar Ali illegally inducted one Abbas Ali in the case property for which she filed Title Suit No.405 of 1985 in the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka for recovery of possession. During the pendency of the said suit Abbas Ali voluntarily handed over possession of the property to her. Her further case is that her vendor Sk. Majnu was all along in Bangladesh and he possessed the house of the disputed plot even after the promulgation of P.O. 16 of 1972. Title Suit No.393 of 1984 was decreed ex parte against the Government and the Government filed Miscellaneous Case No.54 of 1986 under Order 9 Rule 13 for setting aside the ex parte decree which was also dismissed on 26.08.1990. Her further case is that as she obtained a decree by challenging the status of the property in question, the enlistment of the said property as abandoned is against the provision of Section 5(b) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (for short Ordinance 54 of 1985). 

5. Upon hearing the High Court Division discharged the Rule in Writ Petition No.734 of 2002 vide impugned judgment and order dated 12.04.2005. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division the appellant filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.762 of 2013 before this Division. This Division granted leave on 01.03.2015 and hence the instant Civil Appeal. 

6. Mr. Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury, learned Additional Attorney General along with Mr. Md. Mozibur Rahman, learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the appellant have contended that the case property having been included in the list of the abandoned properties and published in the official Gazette under Section 5(1) of the Ordinance 54 of 1985, such inclusion of the property being the conclusive evidence of its abandoned character, the same has been vested in the government with effect from 28.02.1972. The respondent No.2 having failed to rebut this legal presumption by proving the whereabouts of her alleged vendor, the original allottee at the relevant time i.e. on 28.02.1972, thus the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside. The learned Counsels have contended next that the High Court Division erred in law in discharging the Rule misconstruing the provision of Section 5(b) of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 failing to consider that the respondent No.3 admittedly not in possession of the suit property obtained ex parte decree which is a declaratory decree simpliciter without any prayer of recovery of possession and as such the said decree is not within the contemplation of proviso (b) to Section 5 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985. The learned Counsels have argued next that the High Court Division erred in law in failing to consider that the case property could not legally be transferred by the original allottee Sk. Majnu to the respondent No.2 by executing a deed of sale as the said transfer is barred. under Article 6 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (for short P.O. 16 of 1972) and as such the impugned judgment passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. To buttress the submissions the learned counsels for the appellant referred to several case laws reported in 15 BLD(AD) 175; 51 DLR(AD) 42; 53 DLR(AD) 99; 47 DLR (AD) 71. 

7. On the other hand, Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent No.2 has strenuously contended that the presumption under section 5(2) of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 could not arise in this case inasmuch as before the publication of the list including the case property as an abandoned building on 23.09.1986 decree was passed in Title Suit No.393 of 1984 by the First Court of Munsif on 03.03.1985 declaring that the case property was not an abandoned property and hence inclusion of the property in the list of abandoned buildings on 23.09.1986 was expressly prohibited by Article 5(1) (A) of the Ordinance 54 of 1985. The decree of the civil Court declaring that the case property is not an abandoned property attained finality while the decree of civil Court is binding on the Government and as such the Judgment of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. The learned senior Counsel has argued next that the vendor of respondent No.2 is a national of Bangladesh and he was present in Bangladesh during the period from 1972 of 1974, prior to transfer of the case property to respondent No.2 he managed in person the said property and the appellant had no possession in the property. The learned senior Counsel has contended next that the Court of Settlement rightly relied upon the ex parte decree passed by the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka as the said decree attained finality. The Government is not entitled to challenge the validity of the decree before the court of Settlement and there is no scope for the Court of Settlement to scrutinize the documents and to take evidence about the whereabouts of the original lessee and the Court of Settlement acted legally in forming opinion that since there is an ex parte decree no further fact finding is necessary and therefore the Judgment of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. The learned senior Counsel has submitted next that the respondent No.2 has been able to rebut the presumption under section 5(2) of Ordinance 54 of 1985 and has been able to prove that the original allottee was present in Bangladesh and his whereabouts were known and he did not cease to occupy supervise or manage in person the case property and the transfer by Sk. Mojnu to respondent No.2 is valid as per provision of Article 6 of P.O. 16 of 1972 and therefore the judgment of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. The learned senior Counsel has argued that the sale deed dated 11.01.1974 executed and registered in favour of the respondent No.2 conclusively proves that the original allottee was present in Bangladesh till 11.01.1974 as the original allottee appeared before the registration authority to register the deed of sale and hence the presumption under section 5(2) of Ordinance 54 of 1985 has effectively been rebutted m this case, therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is sustainable in law. The learned senior Counsel has lastly submitted that the respondent No.2 did not file the suit for recovery of possession, since the respondent No.2 obtained a decree that the case property is not an abandoned property the Government is not entitled to retain possession of the case property and having taken possession illegally is under a legal obligation to restore possession of the case property to the respondent No.2 and as such the judgment passed by the High Court Division does not call for interference. 

8. We have considered the submissions of the learned Counsels for both the sides, perused the impugned judgment and order dated 12.04.2005 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.734 of 2002 as well as other materials on record. 

9. It is admitted by both the parties that the plot in question originally belonged to the government. It is also admitted that the said plot was given lease by the government to one Sk. Majnu vide Lease Deed No.3099 dated 21.05.1964 for a period of 99 years. However, the appellant claims that the property in question is an abandoned property. On the other hand, the respondent No.2 claims that she became the owner of the plot in question from Sk. Majnu by a registered Sale Deed No.301 dated 11.01.1974. Admittedly, there is a building on the disputed plot. Now, the determinant factor in this context while resolving the core dispute between the appellant and respondent No.2 hinges on two fold issues firstly, whether the disputed plot is an abandoned property and secondly, whether the respondent No.2 became a legitimate owner in the suit plot by virtue of the Sale Deed No.301 dated 11.01.1974. 

10. Section 2(c) of Ordinance 54 of 1985 refers to P.O. 16 of 1972 which denotes that an abandoned property means a property as defined in Article 2 of the P.O. 16 of 1972. 

11. Article 2 of the P.O. 16 of 1972 provides the following-
2. In this Order, unless there is any-thing repugnant in the subject or context,- 
(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, super-vise or manage in person his property, including-
(i) any property owned by any per-son who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh; 
(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking Over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order,1972 (Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972), but does not include-
(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh; 
(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force. 

12. It is advantageous to mention Section 5(2) of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 which is stated below-
5 (1) The Government shall, after the commencement of this Ordinance and before the 31st day of December, 1988, publish, from time to time, in the official Gazette,- 
(a) lists of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order; 
(b) lists of buildings in respect of which notices for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said Order have been issued: 
Provided that no such list shall include any building in respect of which-
(a) any decree or order has been passed, at any time before the publication of the list in the official Gazette, by any Court declaring the building not to be an abandoned' property or not to have vested in the Government under the President's Order or declaring the possession by the Government of the building as an abandoned property under that Order to be illegal or invalid or directing the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person, or (b) a suit, appeal, application or other legal proceeding is pending before any Court, immediately before the date of publication of the list in the official Gazette, in which the vesting in, or possession of, the Government of the building as abandoned property under the President's Order has been called in question in any manner whatsoever or any prayer has been made for return, restoration or transfer of the building by the Government or by any officer or authority subordinate to it to any person. 
(2) The lists published under sub-section(1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such. 
 
13. The cumulative effect of the afore-said provisions is that under Article 2(1) of the P.O. 16 of 1972 the government may include any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property in the list of abandoned property while Section 5 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 lays down that the government shall publish from time to time, in the official Gazette, lists of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the P.O. 16 of 1972. Section 5(2) of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 attaches a legal presumption regarding the list published under sub-Section (1) as conclusive evidence to the effect that the enlisted property is an abandoned property. However, such presumption is subject to rebuttal by the claimant of title in the said property and the burden of proof shifts on him. 

14. In this regard, we find a good deal of support in the case of Govt. of Bangladesh vs. Md. Jalil and others 15 BLD (AD) (1995)175. It has observed by this Division that-
14. The High Court Division in our opinion, started with a wrong premise holding that the presumption of correctness of the entries in the Gazette notification does not absolve the Government from denying the facts alleged by the claimant or from disclosing the basis of treating the property as abandoned property when it is disputed. Section 5(2) of the Ordinance clearly provides that the list published under sub-section(1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such. Section 7 says that a person claiming any right or interest in any such building may make an application to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the building from such list etc. on the ground that the building is not an abandoned building and has not vested in the Government under P.O. No.16 of 1972 or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that order. The onus, therefore, is squarely on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant.  

15. In view of the above decision as well as relevant provisions of law it is manifest that the respondent No.2 is burdened with the proving of fact that Sk. Majnu was available in Bangladesh on 28.02.1972 when P.O. 16 of 1972 came into force and as such the property is not an abandoned property. Having gone through the judgment of the Court of Settlement as well as other materials on record it is transparent that the respondent No.2 could not prove that Sk. Majnu was available in Bangladesh on 28.02.1972. Admittedly the property was leased out by the government to Sk. Majnu for a period of 99 years vide Lease Deed No.3099 dated 21.05.1964. From a bare reading of the copy of the aforesaid Lease Deed filed in the additional paper book it discloses that said Sk. Majnu was given lease of the said property as he was a displaced person from India and he needed rehabilitation. In the given backdrop Sk. Majnu being a displaced person from India having taken lease of the property from the government of the then East Pakistan now Bangladesh in the year 1964 might not be available in Bangladesh on 28.02.1972 when P.O. 16 of 1972 came into force. Despite according to law the respondent No.2 is under strict obligation to prove the existence of Sk. Majnu in Bangladesh on 28.02.1972. No convincible evidence was adduced by the respondent No.2 in this regard. The respondent No.2 did not even state the whereabouts of Sk. Majnu let alone producing him before the Court at any point of time. The respondent No.2 utterly failed to prove that Sk. Majnu was present in Bangladesh on 28.02:1972 and further failed to prove that Sk. Majnu used to occupy, supervise or manage in person the property in question on 28.02.1972 when P.O. 16 of 1972 came into force. In failure of the respondent No.2 to prove the aforesaid facts we are constrained to hold that the property in question is an abandoned property. 

16. The respondent No.2 asserts her title in the property in question by way of Deed No.301 dated 11.01.1974 from Sk. Majnu. Now a pertinent question arises how a person can transfer an abandoned property. Article 6 of the P.O. 16 of 1972 lays down that-
6. No person shall, except in accordance with the provisions of this Order or any rules made thereunder, transfer any abandoned property in any manner or create any charge or encumbrance on such property, and any transfer made or charge or encumbrance created in contravention of this Order shall be null and void. 

17. Having regard to the above legal provisions it is conspicuous that unlike other transfer an abandoned property can only be transferred with the prior permission of the government. But the respondent No.2 could neither show such permission nor even state whether any permission from the government was taken at all. 

18. We are surprised to notice from the perusal of the Deed No.301 dated 11.01.1974 that the first page of which was written on a stamp paper of 150 taka over which 'Bangladesh' was imprinted while the 2nd page of the said deed was written on a stamp paper valuing 12 rupees 50 paisa over which 'Pakistan' was imprinted. But the fact remains that after the independence of Bangladesh more particularly on 11.01.1974 no sale deed according to law can be executed and registered on a stamp paper of Pakistan. Thus, the Sale Deed No.301 by virtue of which the respondent No.2 claims her title in the disputed property is not a valid instrument carrying legal value in the eye of law. The aforesaid anomaly speaks volume that the respondent No.1 in collaboration with the vested quarters manufactured the alleged Sale Deed by false personation of Sk. Majnu mala fide only to grab the valuable government property. The respondent No.2 managed to get away the said forgery from the notice of the High Court Division as well as the Court of Settlement and lower Civil Court by surreptitious practice. 

19. From the record the respondent No.2 appears to claim that after refusal by the Ministry of Public Works and Housing to mutate the disputed property in her name she filed Title Suit No.393 of 1984 before the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka for declaration the property is not an abandoned property and also for declaration of title and for direction to mutate the land in her name. The said suit was decreed ex parte against the Government and the Government filed Miscellaneous Case No.54 of 1986 under Order 9 Rule 13 for setting aside the ex parte decree which was also dismissed on 26.08.1990. Generally, a decree passed by any Court of law must be respected but in the case in hand the decrees as referred by the respondent No.2 are not backed by law. Since the respondent No.2 could not acquire title in the disputed property by virtue of Sale Deed No.301 we are led to irresistible conclusion that the respondent No.2 obtained the decrees in Title Suit No.393 of 1984 and other suits/ case collusively resorting to fraud with an ill-motive of establishing her title in an abandoned property through the Courts of law. Therefore, those decrees are nullity in the eye of law having no binding force at all. 

20. Moreover, since the respondent No.2 could not acquire title in the disputed plot she had no scope to get a lawful possession in the disputed property. It divulges from the record that the respondent No.2 filed the Title Suit No.393 of 1984 for declaration that the property is not an abandoned property. In the given backdrop, an important question arises whether a declaratory decree simpliciter without any prayer for recovery of possession comes within the contemplation of proviso (a) to Section 5 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985. The question has been fairly answered by this Division in the case of Bangladesh Vs. Anwar Ahmed and others 51 DLR(AD) 42. This Division observed in the said case that-
"18  Proviso (a) to section 5 contemplates a legally enforceable decree. The ex parte decree obtained by the writ petitioner is a declaratory decree simpliciter without any prayer for recovery of possession, when, admittedly, the writ petitioner was not in possession thereof. Such a decree is not within the contemplation of proviso (a) to section 5." 

21. Therefore, it is settled law that where a person is not in possession of the property in question a declaratory decree simpliciter without any prayer for recovery of possession obtained prior to the publication of list of abandoned buildings will not safeguard the property to be included in the list of abandoned buildings. In the case in hand, palpably the respondent No.2 had no possession in the disputed property and as such the ex parte decree for declaration simpliciter without any prayer for recovery of possession obtained by her in Title Suit No.393 of 1984 will not be a bar in including the property in question in the list of abandoned property. 

22. In the light of the aforesaid reasons as well as an elaborate discussion regarding the factual and legal aspects of the case the impugned judgment and order dated 12.04.2005 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.734 of 2002 warrants interference by this Division. Therefore, we find merit in the submissions of the learned senior Counsel for the appellant. In the prevailing circumstances, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division cannot stand at all in, the eye of law. 

23. Accordingly, the instant Civil Appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.
 
24. The judgment and order dated 12.04.2005 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 734 of 2002 is set aside.
